_about: Plain-English notes on every table in exo.db, shown on the Terrain map's table window (routes/terrain_tables.py serves them; frontend/src/features/terrain/ shows them). One entry per table: `holds` = what information is in it; `source` = where its rows come from, including the indirect path a code scan can't see; `kind` = 'mirror' (a copy that can be wiped and rebuilt from its source), 'record' (the only copy — wiping it loses history), 'store' (the database of record itself), or 'mixed'; `time_column` = the column that says WHEN a row happened, which is what 'newest first' sorts by (null when the table has no such column); `columns` = one entry per column — `holds` says what the column contains, and `values`, for a column that holds a fixed set of categories, says what each value means. Written from the comments beside each CREATE TABLE in sqlstore.py — when a table or column changes there, change its note here. tests/test_terrain_tables.py fails if a table or a column has no entry. Keep these generic: no personal details, this repo is shareable.

docs.holds: Every ordinary collection the app keeps — to-dos, contacts, budget, settings, and dozens more — each stored whole as one row: the collection's name, its entire contents as JSON text, and when it was last written. Few rows, but each one is a whole document.
docs.source: Written by store.py through sqlstore.py every time any page saves a collection. The .json files in the data folder are one-way export copies of these rows, never read back.

name.holds: The collection's name — 'todos', 'contacts', 'budget'. The key: there is exactly one row per collection.

data.holds: The whole collection as one piece of JSON text. This is why the table has few rows but is large: each row is an entire document.

updated_at.holds: When this collection was last saved, in UTC.

habits.holds: One row per habit that has ever existed: its name, which section of the habit list it sits in, whether it is still active, when it started, and — if the owner has said two habits were always the same one — which habit it was merged into.
habits.source: Rebuilt by habitstore.py from the habits_log collection and the habit list. A habit is a row with a stable id, so renaming it doesn't lose its history.

id.holds: The habit's permanent number. Everything else about a habit can change; this never does.

name.holds: What the habit is called right now.

section.holds: Which section of the habit list it sits in, in lowercase. Empty text (never NULL) means no section.

active.holds: Whether the habit is still on the list.

values.0: dropped from the list — its history is kept

started_on.holds: The first day this habit appears in the log.

merged_into.holds: Points at another habit's id when the owner has said these two were always the same habit. Empty for almost every row. Set by hand, and never touched by a rebuild.

created_at.holds: When this row was first made in the database (UTC) — not when the habit started.

habit_aliases.holds: Every name a habit has ever been logged under, each pointing at the habit it means. This is what keeps old history reachable after a habit is renamed, moved to another section, or dropped from the list.
habit_aliases.source: Rebuilt by habitstore.py alongside the habits table.

alias.holds: One name a habit has been logged under — both old bare names and the current 'section|name' form.

habit_id.holds: Which habit that name means. Points at habits.id.

habit_entries.holds: One row per habit per day: done, missed, or skipped — plus whether that answer was actually logged or only inferred. The raw log can only say 'done', so 'didn't do it' and 'wasn't on the list yet' look identical there; this table tells them apart, and says which answers are guesses.
habit_entries.source: Rebuilt by habitstore.py from the habits_log collection.

habit_id.holds: Which habit. Points at habits.id. Together with `date` it identifies the row: one row per habit per day.

status.holds: What happened with the habit that day.

values.missed: it was on the list and not done

source.holds: How sure this row is. Never mix the two in a claim.

values.inferred: worked out by habitstore — the raw log can only record 'done', so a miss has to be deduced

expense_categories.holds: The short list of spending categories, each with an id. It is its own table, rather than a word repeated on every expense, so an expense can point at a category and a form can offer a dropdown.
expense_categories.source: Rebuilt by expensestore.py from the categories used in the expenses collection.

id.holds: The category's number, which expenses point at.

name.holds: The category's name. Each name appears once.

expenses.holds: One row per transaction: the date, the amount in whole cents (never a decimal, so sums can't drift), whether money went out or came in, its category, the bank's memo line, a title, a receipt reference, and where the row came from.
expenses.source: Rebuilt by expensestore.py from the expenses collection, which the budget pages edit. Ids are kept the same in both places so a row here and an entry there are provably the same expense.

id.holds: The expense's id, kept identical to its id in the expenses collection so the two are provably the same entry.

date.holds: The day of the transaction, as YYYY-MM-DD.

amount_cents.holds: The amount in whole cents — 1250 means $12.50. Never a decimal, so sums can't drift. Always positive: `direction` says which way the money went.

direction.holds: Which way the money moved. Needed because every amount is stored positive.

category_id.holds: Which category it belongs to. Points at expense_categories.id. Empty when uncategorised.

description.holds: The bank's raw memo line for the transaction.

title.holds: A readable name for the expense, when one was given.

receipt.holds: A reference to a saved receipt, when there is one.

source.holds: Where the row came from — typed in by hand ('manual') or an import.

created_at.holds: When this row was made in the database (UTC) — not the transaction date.

files.holds: One row per file that git has ever seen in either repo (plus files a session touched that were never committed): which repo, the path it has now, when it was first and last seen, and when it was deleted if it was. A file keeps its id through renames — the path is a fact about it, not its identity.
files.source: Built by codestore.py by walking both repos' git history and the session footprints. Git stays the truth; this is a queryable index over it.

id.holds: The file's permanent number. It survives renames — the path is a fact about the file, not its identity.

repo.holds: Which repo the file is in.

path.holds: The path the file has now, or had last if it's been deleted. Not unique on purpose: two different files can have worn the same path in different eras.

first_seen.holds: When git first saw the file. Empty means git never has — an agent touched a file that was never committed.

last_seen.holds: When git last saw the file change.

deleted_at.holds: When a commit deleted the file. Empty means it is still alive; cleared again if a later commit brings the path back.

file_paths.holds: Every path any file has ever had, each pointing at the file it belonged to. This is how an old path in an old commit still finds the right file after a rename.
file_paths.source: Built by codestore.py alongside the files table.

repo.holds: Which repo. Together with `path` it identifies the row.

path.holds: One path some file has had, at any point in history.

file_id.holds: Which file wore that path. Points at files.id. When a path was reused, the most recent owner wins.

commits.holds: One row per git commit in either repo: its id, which repo, when it was authored (as both a number for maths and local text for joining to journal days), the author, and the subject line.
commits.source: Built by codestore.py from git log. The Terrain map's heat comes from here.

sha.holds: The commit's git id — the long hex string git gives every commit.

repo.holds: Which repo the commit is in.

authored_ts.holds: When it was authored, as seconds since 1970 — the form that's easy to do arithmetic on.

authored_at.holds: The same moment as local date-and-time text — the form that joins to journal days and habit dates.

subject.holds: The first line of the commit message.

commit_files.holds: One row for every file changed in every commit: which commit, which file, what happened to it (added, modified, deleted, renamed), and how many lines were added and removed. By far the biggest table, because it is commits multiplied by files. 'Which files change together' is a question asked of this table.
commit_files.source: Built by codestore.py from git log. It is the link between commits and files.

sha.holds: Which commit. Points at commits.sha. Together with `file_id` it identifies the row.

file_id.holds: Which file that commit changed. Points at files.id.

status.holds: What the commit did to the file — git's own one-letter code.

added.holds: Lines added. Empty means git couldn't count (a binary file) — which is different from 0.

removed.holds: Lines removed. Empty means git couldn't count — different from 0.

sessions.holds: One row per agent conversation held in the Observatory: its id, title, which bot, which room (lane) it lives in, when it started and when it was last active.
sessions.source: Built by codestore.py from the conversation index the Observatory keeps in the bot_chats data folder.

id.holds: The conversation's id — its start time, like 2026-09-19.140939.

bot.holds: Which bot the conversation is with.

lane.holds: Which room of the Observatory it lives in — personal, coding, or orchestra.

last_at.holds: When it was last active. A conversation is a container, not an activity — many stay open for days — so this says little about when the owner was actually at the keyboard; session_turns does.

session_files.holds: Which files each agent conversation touched, and how: counts of writes, reads and creates, and when it last touched the file. This is what lets the map ring an agent's footprint.
session_files.source: Built by codestore.py from the footprints sidecar (scripts/extract_footprints.py harvests it from the transcripts).

session_id.holds: Which conversation. Points at sessions.id. Together with `file_id` it identifies the row.

file_id.holds: Which file it touched. Points at files.id.

writes.holds: How many times the agent edited or wrote the file.

reads.holds: How many times it read the file.

creates.holds: How many times it created the file.

last.holds: When it last touched the file. In UTC — unlike most times in this database, which are local.

session_turns.holds: One row per message the owner sent to an agent: which conversation, its position, the moment it was sent, and whether that message also went into the journal. No message text — only the moment — because this table exists to be drawn on a timeline.
session_turns.source: Built by codestore.py from the conversation transcripts. Rebuilt from scratch each time, which is safe because the transcripts are the truth.

seq.holds: The message's position in the transcript. Part of the key, because two messages sent in the same second are still two turns.

ts.holds: The moment the message was sent, in local time. No message text is stored — only the moment.

journaled.holds: Whether this message also went into the journal, as flagged by the capture hook when it made the card.

job_runs.holds: What the scheduled background jobs actually did: one row per run — which job, when it started and finished, whether it worked, did nothing, failed or was switched off, and how many things it looked at, acted on, and failed on. A run with no finish time is either still going or died, which is the silent-failure alarm. Quiet every-minute runs are folded into one hourly heartbeat row so the noise doesn't pile up.
job_runs.source: Written by jobstore.py as each job runs. A run is an event that happened once, so this can never be rebuilt — finished days are copied to JSON files under the data folder's job_runs/ as the backup.

job.holds: Which scheduled job ran. Matches the job's id on the Automations page.

started.holds: When the run began, in local time. The row is written at the START, which is what makes a crash visible.

finished.holds: When the run ended. Empty means it never closed: still going, or it died. An old row with no finish time is the silent-failure alarm.

values.noop: woke up and found nothing to do
values.failed: raised an error or reported a failure
values.skipped: deliberately stood down because the job is switched off — not a failure

ticks.holds: How many quiet runs this one row stands for. Jobs that run every minute and do nothing are folded into one heartbeat row per hour, and this counts them.

looked.holds: How many things the run considered. Empty means this job doesn't count that — different from 0.

acted.holds: How many things it changed. Empty means not counted.

failed.holds: How many things it errored on. Empty means not counted.

note.holds: A short line from the job about what happened.

detail.holds: Extra detail as JSON text, for anything the three counters can't carry.

filer_nominations.holds: Every filing suggestion the filer has made: which file, where it was at the time, a fingerprint of its contents, which model looked at it, what the model says it saw, where it proposed to file it and why, how confident it was, the options it considered and passed over, the latest verdict, and whether the move was actually carried out.
filer_nominations.source: Written by filerstore.py as the filer runs. Kept as a training record of proposals, so it is never rebuilt; finished days are copied to JSON as the backup.

run_id.holds: Which job run produced it. Points at job_runs.id.

file_id.holds: Which file it is about — the file's identity, so the suggestion still points at the right file after it's moved. Points at files.id.

path.holds: Where the file lived at the moment it was nominated.

sha256.holds: A fingerprint of the file's contents. The same bytes give the same fingerprint under any name, which is how duplicate uploads are recognised.

observed.holds: When the filer looked at the file, in local time.

model.holds: Which AI model made the suggestion.

saw.holds: The model's own description of what it saw in the file, in its words.

proposal.holds: Where it proposed to file it, as JSON: destination, front, and action.

confidence.holds: How confident it was, from 0 to 1.

alternatives.holds: The options it considered and didn't pick, with their scores, as JSON.

verdict.holds: The latest ruling on the suggestion — a copy of the newest row in filer_verdicts, kept here so the review queue is one quick lookup.

values.redirected: right idea, wrong destination — the ruling says where it should go

applied.holds: Whether the file was actually moved — kept separate from whether it was accepted.

applied_at.holds: When the move was carried out.

filer_verdicts.holds: Every ruling made on a filing suggestion: accepted, rejected, or redirected, when, by whom, a note, and — for a redirect — where it should have gone instead. Rulings are only ever added, never overwritten, so a change of mind is kept as history.
filer_verdicts.source: Written by filerstore.py when a suggestion is judged. The rejections and redirects are the most valuable rows: they are the examples of where the boundary is.

nomination_id.holds: Which suggestion was ruled on. Points at filer_nominations.id. One suggestion can have several rulings over time — a changed mind is kept, not overwritten.

by.holds: Who ruled. Only the owner's own rulings count as ground truth for training.

note.holds: A note left with the ruling.

corrected.holds: For a redirect: where it should have gone, as JSON. The single most valuable column here — it holds the right answer beside the wrong one.

cards.holds: One row per journal card: its id, the journal day, the full timestamp, who wrote it (the owner or the Keeper), what kind of card it is, which card it answers, which session it came from, and the text itself. It also tracks presence: when the card's file was first and last seen, whether it was deliberately deleted, and whether it has gone missing without explanation — a loud alarm, because the journal promises never to lose a card.
cards.source: Built by cardstore.py from the card markdown files in the vault, which stay the truth. The pond and the Terrain map's pond tile are drawn from this table.

id.holds: The card's id: its date, time, a letter for who wrote it, and sometimes a counter — like 2026-08-02.0808b.

day.holds: The journal day, as YYYY-MM-DD, split out of the id so questions about a day are easy.

ts.holds: The full moment it was written, in local time.

kind.holds: What sort of card it is, from the card's own header.

reply_to.holds: The id of the card this one answers — how a Keeper question and the owner's answer are paired.

session.holds: Which journaling session the card came from.

refs.holds: References the card carries, as a JSON list.

body.holds: The text of the card itself.

first_seen.holds: When the sync first found this card's file. A sync-clock time, not the card's own time.

last_seen.holds: When the sync last found the file still there.

deleted_at.holds: Set when the file is gone AND there is a record of the owner deleting it. Empty for a living card.

missing_since.holds: Set when the file is gone with NO record of why. This should always be empty — a value here is the journal's integrity alarm.

card_tags.holds: Which tags are on which journal card — one row per card-and-tag pair, nothing else. A plain pair table, so 'every card tagged x' is one quick lookup.
card_tags.source: Built by cardstore.py from the tags written in each card file.

card_id.holds: Which card. Points at cards.id. Together with `tag` it identifies the row.

fronts.holds: The list of life domains ('fronts') that to-dos can belong to: an id, a display name, when it was created, and whether it is officially in the registry — old retired domains still riding on a few to-dos are kept and flagged rather than dropped.
fronts.source: Rebuilt by todostore.py from the fronts registry and from whatever fronts appear on to-dos.

id.holds: The front's short id, which to-dos point at.

registered.holds: Whether it is in the official registry.

values.0: not in the registry — a retired front still riding on a few old to-dos, kept rather than dropped

todos.holds: One row per to-do, wide because a to-do has many facets: its text, which list it is in and its hand-set position there, whether it is done, when it was created, one folded-together completion moment (and which of three older fields that came from), notes, due date and time, duration, place, what it has to wait for, its status, and who or what created it.
todos.source: Rebuilt by todostore.py from the todos collection, which the to-do page edits. The collection stays the truth; this is a mirror for asking questions like 'what got done this week'.

id.holds: The to-do's permanent id — a short hex string, identical to its id in the todos collection.

bucket.holds: Which list it sits in. A fact about the to-do, not its identity — moving it between lists keeps the same row.

position.holds: Its hand-set place within that list, counting from 0.

done.holds: Whether it is ticked off. Kept separately from `bucket` on purpose: an item can be ticked while still sitting in `now`, until the nightly sweep moves it.

finished_on.holds: The day it was finished, folded together from three older fields. Empty means not finished.

finished_time.holds: The time of day it was finished, when known.

finished_source.holds: Which field `finished_on` really came from — so an old day-stamp is never passed off as a precise claim.

values.claimed: the owner said when it was done
values.marked: the moment it was ticked in the app

finished_note.holds: A note left when finishing it.

duration_min.holds: How long it is expected to take, in minutes.

place_id.holds: Which place it has to be done at, when it is tied to one.

after_date.holds: A day it can't start before.

after_id.holds: What it has to wait for — usually another to-do's id, sometimes a hand-written label. Deliberately not a foreign key: a dangling reference here is information, not corruption.

status.holds: A free status word on the to-do, when one is set.

created_at.holds: When this row was made in the database (UTC) — not when the to-do was written.

origin_by.holds: Who created the to-do — the owner or a named agent.

origin_at.holds: When it was created, according to its provenance record.

origin_conv.holds: Which conversation it was created in, when an agent made it.

todo_fronts.holds: Which life domains each to-do belongs to — one row per to-do-and-front pair. A pure join table: both of its columns point at other tables.
todo_fronts.source: Rebuilt by todostore.py from the fronts listed on each to-do.

front.holds: Which life domain it belongs to. Points at fronts.id.

todo_subtasks.holds: The checklist items under a to-do, in order: which to-do, its position, the subtask's own id, its text, and whether it is done.
todo_subtasks.source: Rebuilt by todostore.py from the subtasks inside each to-do.

todo_id.holds: Which to-do this checklist item is under. Points at todos.id. Together with `position` it identifies the row.

position.holds: Its place in the checklist, counting from 0. Carries the identity here, because subtask ids aren't unique.

subtask_id.holds: The subtask's own id from the collection — sometimes a hand-written label.

todo_agent_notes.holds: Notes that agents have left on to-dos: which to-do, its position, which agent said it and when, the text, what it cites, and which conversation it came from.
todo_agent_notes.source: Rebuilt by todostore.py from the agent notes stored on each to-do (todo_provenance.py defines them).

todo_id.holds: Which to-do the note is on. Points at todos.id.

position.holds: Its place among that to-do's agent notes.

refs.holds: What the note cites, as a JSON list. The citation is the point of the note, so it is never dropped.

conv.holds: Which conversation the note came from.

tags.holds: The universal tagging table: one row says 'this subject has this tag, in this namespace'. A subject can be anything — a card, a to-do, a file, a research entry, a thread — and the namespace (front, topic, …) is what lets new kinds of tag be added without changing the table. Each row also records where it came from: set by hand, derived automatically, or proposed by a background job.
tags.source: Written by routes/tags.py when tags are set by hand, and by scripts/backfill_tags.py for the derived ones. The derived rows can be regenerated at any time; the hand-set rows cannot.

subject.holds: What is being tagged — a card, a to-do, a file, a research entry, a thread — written as its kind and id.

ns.holds: The namespace: what KIND of tag this is (a front, a topic, …). New kinds of tag are new values here, with no change to the table.

values.derived: generated automatically — can be regenerated at any time
values.cricket: proposed by a background job and accepted

attention_segments.holds: When the owner was looking at what: one row per unbroken stretch of attention on one tab — which tab, which agent conversation if it was one, when it started and ended, and the day it belongs to. It gives screen time a beginning and an end, so it can be laid beside file writes and journal cards on one timeline.
attention_segments.source: Rebuilt by attentionstore.py from the per-day attention log files under the data folder's attention/, which are the truth.

tab.holds: Which tab of the app was being looked at.

conv.holds: The agent conversation, when the tab was a chat — joins to sessions.id. Empty everywhere else.

started.holds: When this unbroken stretch of attention began, in local time.

ended.holds: When it ended. The length of the stretch is simply `ended` minus `started` — deliberately not stored as its own column, so the two can't disagree.

day.holds: The journal day it belongs to, split out of `started`.

command_runs.holds: Every slash command that was run: when (with the day and hour split out for counting), the command's name and kind, which session and folder it was run from, and how long its arguments were — the length only, not the text.
command_runs.source: Built by commandstore.py by reading the Claude Code transcripts on disk. Re-readable at any time, so it can be dropped and rebuilt.

uuid.holds: The id of the transcript message the command came from. Reading the same line twice can't insert it twice.

day.holds: The day, split out for counting by day.

hour.holds: The hour of day, 0–23, split out for counting by hour.

kind.holds: What sort of command it was.

session_id.holds: Which Claude Code session it was run in.

cwd.holds: Which folder it was run from.

arg_chars.holds: How long its arguments were, in characters — the length only, never the text.

command_sources.holds: Bookkeeping for the command scan: one row per transcript file, saying how far into it has already been read. Transcripts only ever grow at the end, so this lets each scan pick up where the last one stopped instead of re-reading everything.
command_sources.source: Written by commandstore.py as it scans. If wiped, the next scan simply starts from the top.

size.holds: How many bytes of it have already been read. The next scan starts from here.

code_files.holds: Every code file as it stands on disk right now: which repo, its path, its language, how many lines, how many other files it depends on and how many depend on it, when it was parsed, and the error if it couldn't be. 'What is a hub' and 'what is dead code' are read straight off this table.
code_files.source: Built by codegraph.py by parsing the source. Deliberately separate from the files table: that one is git's view through history, this one is the code as it is today.

repo.holds: Which repo. Together with `path` it identifies the row.

path.holds: The file's path, as it is on disk right now.

lang.holds: What the parser treated the file as.

lines.holds: How many lines long it is.

out_degree.holds: How many other files this one depends on.

in_degree.holds: How many other files depend on this one. High means a hub; zero can mean dead code.

parse_error.holds: Why it couldn't be parsed, when it couldn't. The file keeps its row either way, so a parser gap is visible rather than silent.

code_edges.holds: Every dependency between code files: this file imports from that one, and exactly which names cross — not just 'server.py uses store.py' but which parts of it. Dependencies on outside packages are kept too, marked as external.
code_edges.source: Built by codegraph.py by parsing the source, alongside code_files.

repo.holds: The repo of the file doing the importing.

dst_repo.holds: The repo of the file being imported. Empty text means an outside package, like flask or react.

dst.holds: The file, or outside package, being imported.

kind.holds: What sort of dependency it is.

values.import: a static import read out of the source

symbols.holds: Exactly which names cross the edge, as a JSON list — not just that one file uses another, but which parts of it.

traces.holds: One row per captured request followed through the code: a label, where it was taken, what was being done, when it started, how long it took, how many steps were recorded, whether the recording was cut short, and — when one request continued in another process — which trace it continues.
traces.source: Written by runtime_trace.py when a trace is armed from the Terrain map. A recording of a moment that has passed, so it can't be rebuilt; only the newest few are kept.

label.holds: A name given to the trace.

duration_us.holds: How long it took, in millionths of a second.

truncated.holds: Whether the recording hit its size limit.

values.1: cut short — useful, but not complete

pid.holds: The id of the process it was recorded in.

parent_id.holds: The trace this one continues, when one request carried on in another process. The two halves keep separate rows because their clocks aren't comparable.

trace_spans.holds: The individual steps inside a trace, in order: which function in which file called which function in which file, how deep in the call stack, and the start and end times in millionths of a second from the start of the trace.
trace_spans.source: Written by runtime_trace.py alongside each trace, and deleted with it.

trace_id.holds: Which trace this step belongs to. Points at traces.id.

seq.holds: The step's order within the trace.

depth.holds: How deep in the call stack it is — how many calls are wrapped around it.

src_repo.holds: The repo of the calling file.

src.holds: The file the call came from. Empty means it came from outside the app's code entirely — an entry point.

src_func.holds: The function the call came from.

dst_repo.holds: The repo of the file being called.

t0_us.holds: When the step started, in millionths of a second from the start of the trace.

t1_us.holds: When it ended, on the same clock.

notes.holds: One row per note the owner has written on a page — the small capture panels at the bottom of most pages, where friction ("this is bugging me") and wants ("this could…") get jotted down. Both kinds live here together, told apart by a column, with the page it was written on, its words, when it was written, and where it sits in that page's list.
notes.source: Written directly by the app through notestore.py every time a note is added, edited, moved or deleted. This is the first table here that is the DESTINATION rather than a copy: the two notes files in the data folder are one-way exports of these rows, kept current so the hourly backup stays readable, and never read back.

kind.holds: Which of the two panels the note belongs to. Moving a note between them changes this one value, so the note keeps its identity and its date.

values.dev: a note about friction — something that is bugging her
values.idea: a note about a want — something that could exist

id.holds: The note's permanent name. Plain text with no fixed shape: most are generated, but one can be typed by hand.

page.holds: Which page's panel the note was written on. Free text, mostly matching the page names used elsewhere, plus a few that are not pages at all.

text.holds: The note itself, in the owner's own words.

created.holds: When the note was written, to the minute, kept exactly as it was recorded rather than converted.

position.holds: Where the note sits in its page's list. A table has no order of its own, and the date cannot supply one when two notes share a minute — so this is what keeps a note that refers to the one above it in the right place.

questions.holds: A question left on the note by an overnight worker that could not tell what it meant. Cleared when the note is edited, because the amended words answer the question. Empty for most notes.

extra.holds: Anything written onto a note that has no column of its own, kept as JSON so it cannot be silently lost. Normally empty — if it fills up, that is the sign something deserves a real column.

updated_at.holds: When this ROW last changed, in UTC. Only the notes that actually changed are restamped, so this really does answer "when did this note last move".

note_judgments.holds: One row per ruling the owner has made about a note: whether she wants it, is unsure about it, or has refused it — with her own words about why, when she said it, and who wrote the ruling down. A note can be ruled on many times; nothing is ever overwritten, so changing her mind is itself part of the record.
note_judgments.source: Written by the app through notestore.py whenever a verdict is given — from a note's own card, from the morning card, or on her behalf when editing a note reopens a question. The only copy: these are decisions that cannot be regenerated from anything.

note_kind.holds: Which note this ruling is about, first half — the note's kind. Together with note_id it points at exactly one note, and a ruling for a note that does not exist cannot be stored.

note_id.holds: Which note this ruling is about, second half — the note's name. Delete the note and its rulings go with it automatically.

seq.holds: Which ruling this is: the first, the second, and so on. The LAST one is the note's verdict right now. Needed because the timestamp is only accurate to the minute, and a mind can change twice in one minute.

values.approved: she wants it — the green light overnight work runs on
values.unsure: she cannot tell what the note meant. Not a refusal: adding context to the note reopens it
values.denied: she does not want it, with a reason
values.open: never ruled on, or reopened. A note with no rulings at all reads as this too

comment.holds: Her own words about the ruling, when she wrote any. Often the most useful part of the row.

reason.holds: Why something was refused. Only a refusal carries one, and only from a fixed short list — which is what makes refusals countable.

values.outdated: the note no longer describes anything real
values.completed: the thing the note asked for is already done

at.holds: When the ruling was made, to the minute. Kept in whatever form it was recorded, which varies by vintage.

by.holds: Who wrote the ruling down — the owner tapping a button, a card acting on her behalf, or an automatic reopen. This is what keeps a ruling made for her from reading as one she made herself.

extra.holds: Anything on a ruling that has no column of its own, kept as JSON rather than dropped. Normally empty.

tool_calls.holds: Every tool an agent ran: when, which tool, what it was pointed at (the file, the command, the search pattern), the full input as JSON (capped), and once the result came back, how long it took, how big the result was and whether it errored. Subagent calls carry the call that spawned them.
tool_calls.source: Built by toolcallstore.py by reading the Observatory's conversation logs under the data folder's bot_chats/ and Claude Code's own transcripts under ~/.claude/projects. Re-readable at any time, so it can be dropped and rebuilt with scripts/usage_events.py --rebuild.

tool_use_id.holds: The call's own id, the same in both sources. Reading the same call twice can't insert it twice.

source.holds: Which record it was first read from: observatory (the app's own log) or claude (the harness's transcript). Terminal work only ever has the second.

conv.holds: The Observatory conversation, when it was one — joins to sessions.id. Empty for terminal work.

parent_tool_use_id.holds: The Agent call this ran under, when a subagent made it.

at.holds: When the call was made, local time with milliseconds.

day.holds: The day, split out for counting.

name.holds: The tool: Bash, Read, Edit, Grep, Agent …

target.holds: The one handle worth searching: the file, the command, the pattern, the url.

input.holds: The whole input as JSON, cut at 4000 characters.

result_at.holds: When the result came back. Empty if it never did.

duration_ms.holds: How long the tool took, from call to result.

result_chars.holds: How big the result was. The result itself is not copied; the logs hold it.

is_error.holds: 1 if the tool reported an error.

cwd.holds: The folder the session was working in.

model.holds: The model that made the call.

tool_call_sources.holds: Bookkeeping for the tool-call scan: one row per log file, saying how far into it has been read, the last clock seen there, and how many turn results it held so far.
tool_call_sources.source: Written by toolcallstore.py as it scans. If wiped, the next scan starts from the top.

size.holds: How many bytes of it have been read.

last_at.holds: The last timestamp seen in it, so a turn result read on the next scan can still be dated.

results.holds: How many turn results have been read from it — the next one's number.

turn_results.holds: One row per Observatory turn: how it ended, how long it took, and what it cost in tokens and dollars.
turn_results.source: Built by toolcallstore.py from the result event the harness writes at the end of every turn in the bot_chats logs. Re-readable, so it can be dropped and rebuilt.

seq.holds: Which turn of that conversation this was: 1st, 2nd …

at.holds: When the turn ended, taken from the last stamped line before the result.

day.holds: The day, split out for counting.

subtype.holds: success, or the harness's name for how it failed.

stop_reason.holds: Why the model stopped: end_turn, max_tokens …

duration_ms.holds: Wall time of the whole turn.

duration_api_ms.holds: Time spent waiting on the model.

num_turns.holds: How many model round-trips the turn took.

cost_usd.holds: What the harness reckoned the turn cost.

cache_creation_tokens.holds: Tokens written to the prompt cache.

cache_read_tokens.holds: Tokens read back from the cache.

thinking_tokens.holds: Of the output, how many were thinking.

model.holds: The model that served the turn.

ui_events.holds: Every tap on a tracked control and every page open, one row each: what kind, which tab, which conversation if any, which control, and when.
ui_events.source: Rebuilt by uieventstore.py from the per-day event log files under the data folder's ui_events/, which are the truth.

kind.holds: click (a control was tapped) or open (a page came into view).

conv.holds: The agent conversation, when the tab was a chat — joins to sessions.id.

control.holds: The control's tracking name, for a click. Empty for an open.

day.holds: The day, split out for counting.

requests.holds: Every /api/ request the web app served: when, the method and path, which feature it belongs to, the status it returned, how long it took, and which worker served it.
requests.source: Written by requestlog.py from the request itself, in small batches. Nothing else holds these rows: the access log they replace rotates and drops lines across workers. Never rebuilt.

at.holds: When it was served, local time with milliseconds.

day.holds: The day, split out for counting.

feature.holds: The first part of the path after /api/ — habits, todos, observatory — the same word the daily usage counts use.

duration_ms.holds: How long the app took to answer.

pid.holds: The worker process that served it.
